title: FedReason: Large Language Models as Weight-Space Meta-Aggregators for Heterogeneous Federated Learning

target_networks.name: ResNet-18 (CIFAR variant) global and client models

headline_result.text: An LLM that reads client weights in a sandbox and writes aggregation programs beat FedAvg by 1.26 pp on average over 12 paired label-skew runs, but did not beat SCAFFOLD or FLTrust, and without proxy feedback accuracy fell from 73.8% to 38.8% in one seed.
headline_result.quote: Across 12 paired label-skew runs it beat FedAvg by 1.26 percentage points on average (10 wins), and a control that spends the same per-round proxy budget on choosing among standard rules by 1.08 points.

key_claims.claim: Against ProxySel, a control spending the same per-round proxy budget on choosing among standard rules, the gain was about 1 pp with a wide interval.
key_claims.quote: Against ProxySel, which spends the same per-round proxy budget on choosing among three standard rules, the mean gain was 1.08 pp (95% CI 0.01 to 2.15) with 9 wins, 1 tie and 2 losses (p = 0.064).

key_claims.claim: SCAFFOLD, which changes client training, was the most accurate method in every label-skew setting.
key_claims.quote: SCAFFOLD was the most accurate method in all four settings.

key_claims.claim: Under sign-flipping attack the LLM excluded all three attackers from round 1 based on update norms and cosines, without excluding honest clients.
key_claims.quote: FedReason gave the sign-flipping clients 0.43% of the aggregate on average and excluded all three from round 1 in both seeds, without excluding any honest client

key_claims.claim: Proxy feedback mattered far more than weight access: removing proxy feedback cost 35 points, withholding weights about 6, each in a single seed.
key_claims.quote: In the ablations, removing proxy feedback cost 35 points and withholding the weights about six, each in one seed, while the transcripts show that the LLM’s inferences can be wrong.

key_claims.claim: The LLM misread honest narrow-width clients as label-flip attackers and excluded them, which damaged the sub-model.
key_claims.quote: In the CIFAR-10 width-heterogeneous run with seed 0, the LLM read strongly negative class-9 bias changes of clients 3 and 5 (both × 12 ) as label-flip poisoning

key_claims.claim: A 60-round run cost 0.79 USD in API fees on average.
key_claims.quote: A 60-round run with six invocations cost 0.79 USD on average (0.56 to 1.26 USD).

limitations_stated.text: The system prompt was written knowing the evaluated heterogeneity types; gains may partly come from prompt domain knowledge.
limitations_stated.quote: Part of FedReason’s gains may come from domain knowledge in the prompt rather than from the analysis of the weights

limitations_stated.text: Few seeds; ablations rest on a single seed; outputs cannot be made deterministic.
limitations_stated.quote: Three seeds expose only large effects, and the ablations rest on a single seed each.

limitations_stated.text: Only simple non-adaptive attacks were tested.
limitations_stated.quote: The attacks we evaluated are simple and non-adaptive.

notes_for_review: A carefully controlled application of the Sparks read-then-write idea to federated aggregation: the LLM reads ResNet-18 client weights through a sandbox and writes aggregation code, with 14 baselines, a budget-matched non-LLM control (ProxySel) and ablations removing weights or proxy feedback. Gains are about one point and not significant after correction; the method loses to SCAFFOLD and FLTrust, and the single-seed ablation suggests black-box proxy probing does most of the work. The paper itself is candid about wrong inferences and privacy leakage to the model provider. Code is promised only upon publication.
